doc_description: This document serves as a comprehensive guideline for the management of glomerular diseases, detailing evidence-based recommendations, diagnostic criteria, treatment strategies, and the importance of individualized patient care across various conditions, including Immunoglobulin A nephropathy, lupus nephritis, and membranous nephropathy, while emphasizing the need for ongoing research and collaboration among healthcare professionals.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary: The partial document is a supplement to the journal "Kidney International," specifically focusing on the "KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases." It includes editorial information, a list of editorial board members, and details about the journal's scope, which encompasses kidney research, clinical studies, and original research in nephrology. The document outlines submission guidelines for authors, subscription rates, and contact information for various inquiries, including advertising and permissions. It emphasizes the importance of independent verification in medical practices and clarifies that the views expressed do not necessarily reflect those of the International Society of Nephrology or Elsevier. The publication is sponsored by Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO).

Kidney International is devoted to kidney research. It aims to inform the
researcher, the clinical investigator, and the practicing nephrologist on all aspects
of kidney research. These include the latest clinical studies on emerging
developments in nephrology and the highest level of original research studies in
clinical and basic kidney research. The journal re ﬂects the ﬁeld through critical
reviews, commentaries, original articles, remarkable images, news features,
guidelines, and problem-focused articles for the diagnosis and treatment of
kidney patients.

Medica, Index Medicus/Medline, Science Citation Index, Current Contents/Life

CABS, Biological Abstracts, Global Health, EBSCO, Adonis, and PASCAL.

structure.title: KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases
structure.summary: The partial document outlines the KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases, sponsored by Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO). It emphasizes the importance of independent verification of medical information and the responsibility of practitioners to rely on their own expertise. The document includes a comprehensive structure with sections such as an introduction, summary of recommendations, and detailed chapters on various glomerular diseases, including Immunoglobulin A nephropathy, membranous nephropathy, nephrotic syndrome, and lupus nephritis, among others. It also discusses the methods for guideline development, acknowledges contributors, and provides references. The guideline aims to provide evidence-based recommendations for the management of glomerular diseases while clarifying that the views expressed do not necessarily reflect those of the International Society of Nephrology or Elsevier.

structure.title: Tables, figures, and supplementary material
structure.summary: The partial document outlines the KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases. It includes various sections such as tables, figures, and supplementary materials, as well as a foreword and updates to the guideline format. The document presents a comprehensive overview of recommendations and practice points for managing different types of glomerular diseases, including Immunoglobulin A nephropathy, membranous nephropathy, nephrotic syndrome in children, minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, infection-related glomerulonephritis, and lupus nephritis. Each chapter provides detailed recommendations based on systematic reviews and evidence, including treatment options and management strategies. The guideline development process is also discussed, emphasizing adherence to standards for trustworthy clinical practice guidelines. Additionally, the document includes biographical information about the KDIGO Executive Committee and acknowledgments for contributions to the guideline.

The document concludes with an assurance of the guideline's utility for clinicians treating glomerular diseases worldwide.

With the growing awareness that chronic kidney disease (CKD)
is a major global health problem, Kidney Disease: Improving
Global Outcomes (KDIGO) was established in 2003 with the
stated mission “to improve the care and outcomes of patients
with kidney disease worldwide through promoting coordina-tion, collaboration, and integration of initiatives to develop andimplement clinical practice guidelines. ”
Since 2003, KDIGO has developed a catalog of clinical
practice guidelines informing the care of patients with, or atrisk of developing, kidney diseases. Recently, KDIGO published
one new guideline on Diabetes Management in CKD and
updated their Management of Blood Pressure in CKD guide-line. The last in the series is the update to the Management ofGlomerular Diseases guideline. All 3 guidelines will be pre-sented using a new guideline format.
Glomerular diseases, excluding diabetic nephropathy, ac-
count for about 25% of the cases of CKD worldwide. Giventhe magnitude of long-term morbidity from glomerular dis-
eases, and in particular, their frequent manifestation in
younger patients, it is critical that they be diagnosed ef ﬁ-
ciently, and that management is optimized to control diseaseand prevent progressive kidney disease.
KDIGO published its Clinical Practice Guideline for
Glomerulonephritis (GN) in 2012. The guideline was derivedfrom a signi ﬁcant effort by the Work Group to summarize
recommendations for 12 distinct diseases based on evidence
available through November 2011. Since that time, substantial
new evidence has emerged with important implications for therecommendation statements made in this original guideline.
In 2017, KDIGO convened a Controversies Conference on
Glomerular Diseases. The objective of the conference was togather a global panel of multidisciplinary clinical and scien-tiﬁc experts to identify key issues relevant to the optimal
management of primary and secondary glomerular disease.
The goal was to determine best practice treatment and areas
of uncertainties in the treatment of glomerular disease, reviewkey relevant literature published since the KDIGO 2012 GNGuideline, identify topics or issues that warrant revisiting forfuture guideline updating, and outline research needed toimprove GN management. The conclusions from this Con-troversies Conference were published in Kidney International
last year.
1,2Based on this conference, a guideline update was
recommended.
In keeping with KDIGO ’s policy for transparency and
rigorous public review during the guideline developmentprocess, the scope of the 2017 Controversies Conference wasmade available for open commenting prior to the conference.The guideline Work Group members carefully consideredboth the feedback received on the Scope of Work and theoutput of the conference. This guideline was made available
for public review, too, and the Work Group has criticallyreviewed the public input and revised the guideline as
appropriate for the ﬁnal publication.
We thank Jürgen Floege, MD, and Brad H. Rovin, MD, for
leading this important initiative, and we are especially gratefulto all Work Group members who provided a considerableamount of their time and expertise to this endeavor. Inaddition, this Work Group was ably assisted by colleaguesfrom the independent Evidence Review Team (ERT) led byJonathan C. Craig, MBChB, DipCH, FRACP, M Med (ClinEpi), PhD, Martin Howell, PhD, and David J. Tunnicliffe,
PhD, who made this guideline possible.
KDIGO recently appointed Marcello A. Tonelli, MD, SM,
MSc, FRCPC as its ﬁrst Guideline Methods Chair. He was
tasked with improving KDIGO guideline methodology by
reinforcing the linkage between the recommendations and thecorresponding evidence, standardizing the guideline format,reducing unnecessary length, and strengthening the utility ofthe guideline for its users.
To meet these goals, Dr. Tonelli suggested KDIGO work
with MAGICapp, a web-based publishing platform forevidence-based guidelines. The program uses a prede ﬁned
format and allows for direct linkage of the evidence to therecommendation statement, and the generation of patientdecision aids directly from the evidence syntheses used tosupport the guideline. In addition, he introduced theconcept of practice points, a new form of guidance
produced in addition to recommendations. When a sys-
tematic review was not done or was done but did not ﬁnd
sufﬁcient evidence to warrant a recommendation, a practice
point was used to provide guidance to clinicians. Practicepoints do not necessarily follow the same format asrecommendations —for example, they may be formatted as
tables, ﬁgures, or algorithms —and are not graded for
strength or evidence quality.
With Dr. Tonelli ’s guidance and expertise, the use of
MAGICapp, and the adoption of practice points, KDIGO hasseen the update of the Glomerular Diseases Guideline developinto a highly useful document that is rich in guidance whilemaintaining the high-quality standards and rigor for whichKDIGO is best known. The update to the KDIGO guidelineformat is discussed in greater detail below by Dr. Tonelli(Figure 1 ).
In summary, we are con ﬁdent that this guideline will prove

It highlights KDIGO's mission to enhance patient care through the development and implementation of clinical practice guidelines. The document mentions recent updates to guidelines on Diabetes Management in CKD, Management of Blood Pressure in CKD, and Management of Glomerular Diseases, emphasizing the importance of efficient diagnosis and management of glomerular diseases, which account for a substantial portion of CKD cases. It details the process of updating the Clinical Practice Guideline for Glomerulonephritis, including a 2017 Controversies Conference that gathered experts to discuss optimal management practices and identify areas needing further research. Foreword
Kidney International (2021) 100 , S1–S276; https://doi.org/10.1016/j.kint.2021.05.021
With the growing awareness that chronic kidney disease (CKD)
is a major global health problem, Kidney Disease: Improving
Global Outcomes (KDIGO) was established in 2003 with the
stated mission “to improve the care and outcomes of patients
with kidney disease worldwide through promoting coordina-tion, collaboration, and integration of initiatives to develop andimplement clinical practice guidelines. ”
Since 2003, KDIGO has developed a catalog of clinical
practice guidelines informing the care of patients with, or atrisk of developing, kidney diseases. Recently, KDIGO published
one new guideline on Diabetes Management in CKD and
updated their Management of Blood Pressure in CKD guide-line. The last in the series is the update to the Management ofGlomerular Diseases guideline. All 3 guidelines will be pre-sented using a new guideline format.
Glomerular diseases, excluding diabetic nephropathy, ac-
count for about 25% of the cases of CKD worldwide. Giventhe magnitude of long-term morbidity from glomerular dis-
eases, and in particular, their frequent manifestation in
younger patients, it is critical that they be diagnosed ef ﬁ-
ciently, and that management is optimized to control diseaseand prevent progressive kidney disease.
KDIGO published its Clinical Practice Guideline for
Glomerulonephritis (GN) in 2012. The guideline was derivedfrom a signi ﬁcant effort by the Work Group to summarize
recommendations for 12 distinct diseases based on evidence
available through November 2011. Since that time, substantial
new evidence has emerged with important implications for therecommendation statements made in this original guideline.
In 2017, KDIGO convened a Controversies Conference on
Glomerular Diseases. The objective of the conference was togather a global panel of multidisciplinary clinical and scien-tiﬁc experts to identify key issues relevant to the optimal
management of primary and secondary glomerular disease.
The goal was to determine best practice treatment and areas
of uncertainties in the treatment of glomerular disease, reviewkey relevant literature published since the KDIGO 2012 GNGuideline, identify topics or issues that warrant revisiting forfuture guideline updating, and outline research needed toimprove GN management. The conclusions from this Con-troversies Conference were published in Kidney International
last year.
1,2Based on this conference, a guideline update was
recommended.
In keeping with KDIGO ’s policy for transparency and
rigorous public review during the guideline developmentprocess, the scope of the 2017 Controversies Conference wasmade available for open commenting prior to the conference.The guideline Work Group members carefully consideredboth the feedback received on the Scope of Work and theoutput of the conference. This guideline was made available
for public review, too, and the Work Group has criticallyreviewed the public input and revised the guideline as
appropriate for the ﬁnal publication.
We thank Jürgen Floege, MD, and Brad H. Rovin, MD, for
leading this important initiative, and we are especially gratefulto all Work Group members who provided a considerableamount of their time and expertise to this endeavor. Inaddition, this Work Group was ably assisted by colleaguesfrom the independent Evidence Review Team (ERT) led byJonathan C. Craig, MBChB, DipCH, FRACP, M Med (ClinEpi), PhD, Martin Howell, PhD, and David J. Tunnicliffe,
PhD, who made this guideline possible.
KDIGO recently appointed Marcello A. Tonelli, MD, SM,
MSc, FRCPC as its ﬁrst Guideline Methods Chair. He was
tasked with improving KDIGO guideline methodology by
reinforcing the linkage between the recommendations and thecorresponding evidence, standardizing the guideline format,reducing unnecessary length, and strengthening the utility ofthe guideline for its users.
To meet these goals, Dr. Tonelli suggested KDIGO work
with MAGICapp, a web-based publishing platform forevidence-based guidelines. The program uses a prede ﬁned
format and allows for direct linkage of the evidence to therecommendation statement, and the generation of patientdecision aids directly from the evidence syntheses used tosupport the guideline. In addition, he introduced theconcept of practice points, a new form of guidance
produced in addition to recommendations. When a sys-
tematic review was not done or was done but did not ﬁnd
sufﬁcient evidence to warrant a recommendation, a practice
point was used to provide guidance to clinicians. Practicepoints do not necessarily follow the same format asrecommendations —for example, they may be formatted as
tables, ﬁgures, or algorithms —and are not graded for
strength or evidence quality.
With Dr. Tonelli ’s guidance and expertise, the use of
MAGICapp, and the adoption of practice points, KDIGO hasseen the update of the Glomerular Diseases Guideline developinto a highly useful document that is rich in guidance whilemaintaining the high-quality standards and rigor for whichKDIGO is best known. The update to the KDIGO guidelineformat is discussed in greater detail below by Dr. Tonelli(Figure 1 ).
In summary, we are con ﬁdent that this guideline will prove
useful to clinicians treating people with glomerular diseasethroughout the world. Once again, we thank the Work GroupCo-Chairs and members and all those who contributed to thisvery important KDIGO activity.

The Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the
Management of Glomerular Diseases is an update to the KDIGO 2012 guideline on the topic. The
aim is to assist clinicians caring for individuals with glomerular disease, both adults and children.
The scope includes various glomerular diseases, including IgA nephropathy (IgAN) and IgAvasculitis (IgAV), membranous nephropathy, nephrotic syndrome in children, minimal changedisease (MCD), focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), infection-related glomerulonephritis(GN), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis, lupus nephritis, and
anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibody GN. In addition, this guideline will
be the ﬁrst to address the subtype of complement-mediated diseases. Each chapter follows the
same format providing guidance related to diagnosis, prognosis, treatment, and special situations.The goal of the guideline is to generate a useful resource for clinicians and patients by providingactionable recommendations with valuable infographics based on a rigorous formal systematicliterature review. Another aim is to propose research recommendations for areas where there aregaps in knowledge. The guideline targets a broad audience of clinicians treating glomerulardisease while being mindful of implications for policy and cost. Development of this guideline
update followed an explicit process of evidence review. Treatment approaches and guideline
recommendations are based on systematic reviews and evidence synthesis of relevant studies, andappraisal of the quality of the evidence and the strength of recommendations followed the“Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation ”(GRADE) approach.
Limitations of the evidence are discussed, with areas of future research also presented.

Kidney International (2021) 100 , S1–S276 S27Introduction
Glomerular disease, be it primary or secondary, occurring in
the setting of systemic autoimmune diseases, infections,drugs, or malignancy, affects individuals of all ages. In mostkidney failure registries, glomerular diseases account forabout 20% –25% of the prevalent cases. However, in children,
teenagers, and young adults, glomerular disease is one of the
most common causes of irreversible kidney damage and, as
such, is not only a source of personal suffering but also amajor socioeconomic problem.
In 2012, KDIGO published its ﬁrst-ever guideline on the
management of glomerular diseases. In the 8 years that havepassed, several major discoveries have been made that relateto our understanding of the pathogenesis, diagnosis, andtherapy of glomerular disease. The unequivocal proof that
primary membranous nephropathy is an autoimmune dis-
ease, the uncovering of the role of complement in glomer-ulopathies from dense deposit disease to ANCA-associatedvasculitis, and the demonstration that targeting B cells iseffective for treating diseases mediated by pathogenic (auto)antibodies are examples of some of the most important ad-vances. Thus, an update of the 2012 guideline is appropriateand more urgent as ever.
In this guideline, we have largely maintained the topics
covered in the ﬁrst edition, focusing on the most common
adult and pediatric glomerulonephritides (i.e., IgAN,membranous nephropathy, nephrotic syndrome includingminimal change disease and FSGS, and infection-relatedglomerulonephritis [GN]), as well as systemic immuno-logic diseases (i.e., lupus nephritis, ANCA-associated vascu-litis, and anti-GBM antibody GN). We have expanded the
chapter on General principles for the management of glomer-
ular disease that discusses supportive therapies appropriate
for all glomerular diseases that supplement the more speci ﬁc
immunosuppressive treatments for each disease. Consistent
with new ﬁndings on disease pathogenesis, the updated
Membranous nephropathy chapter now provides an in-depth
discussion of monitoring pathogenic autoantibodies in dis-ease management. We have replaced the chapter heading on
membranoproliferative GN (MPGN) with a new chapter
entitled Immunoglobulin- and complement-mediated glomer-
ular diseases with an MPGN pattern of injury .T h ec h a p t e r
onAntineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated
vasculitis compares and contrasts B cell –targeted therapies
with traditional cytotoxic drugs. The chapter on Focal
segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) has been reorganized to
help clinicians more accurately differentiate between FSGS
mediated by a soluble factor that may be amenable to
immunosuppression, and condi tions with FSGS-like histol-
ogy, for which immunosuppression should not be used.Nephrotic syndrome in children takes advantage of severalnew trials that have de ﬁned duration of immunosuppres-
sion, and this chapter has been written to closely align withrecommendations from the International PediatricNephrology Association (IPNA).
Although the present guideline is the most extensive
KDIGO guideline to date, covering a large array of diseases,there are a few remaining glomerular diseases not addressed.Speci ﬁcally, very rare GN types, such as ﬁbrillary GN,
immunotactoid GN, and IgM GN, for example, are notcovered, related in part to space and resource restrictions,but particularly because of the lack of controlled trials toguide treatment. Our focus on immune-mediated glomer-
ular disease has led to the exclusion of other important
entities, such as amyloidosis and immunoglobulin deposi-tion diseases, Alport syndrome, and thromboticmicroangiopathies.
The guideline primarily considers questions of clinical
management for which high-quality scienti ﬁc evidence is
available. It is not meant to replace textbooks. Rather, incollaboration with an Evidence Review Team, the Work
Group reassessed questions posed in the 2012 guideline
version and identi ﬁed several issues that have remained
clinically pressing and for which there is now at least someevidence base from which to make defensible recommenda-tions. The chapter on General principles for the management of
glomerular disease links this guideline with other KDIGO
guidelines, the most important of which cover the manage-ment of hypertension associated with chronic kidney disease
(KDIGO Guideline for the Management of Blood Pressure in
CKD: https://kdigo.org/guidelines/blood-pressure-in-ckd/ ).
At the end of each chapter, a research agenda has also beenincluded and is intended to provide a roadmap for futureinvestigation based on our comprehensive review of thecurrent state of clinical evidence.
The majority of glomerular diseases are classi ﬁed as rare
diseases, and consequently, there is a paucity of randomized
controlled trials on which to base ﬁrm recommendations.
Given this situation, evidence-based recommendations have
been supplemented with practice points, based on retro-spective analyses, registry data, and consensus of expertopinion to ﬁll in management gaps when there was insuf ﬁ-
cient evidence to make a formal recommendation. The readerwill notice that most of this guideline is comprised of practicepoints. This should be taken as a challenge to the clinical
investigators of the nephrology community to develop novel
clinical trial designs, such as basket trials, umbrella trials,biomarker-driven trials, and n-of-1 trials, to implement theproposed research agenda in the absence of a suf ﬁcient
number of patients to carry out traditional prospective ran-domiz
ed controlled trials.
As Co-Chairs, we are more than grateful to the Work
Group, Evidence Review Team, and KDIGO staff for their
outstanding contributions to the creation of this extensiveintroduction www.kidney-international.org

entities, such as amyloidosis and immunoglobulin deposi-tion diseases, Alport syndrome, and thromboticmicroangiopathies.
The guideline primarily considers questions of clinical
management for which high-quality scienti ﬁc evidence is
available. It is not meant to replace textbooks. Rather, incollaboration with an Evidence Review Team, the Work
Group reassessed questions posed in the 2012 guideline
version and identi ﬁed several issues that have remained
clinically pressing and for which there is now at least someevidence base from which to make defensible recommenda-tions. The chapter on General principles for the management of
glomerular disease links this guideline with other KDIGO
guidelines, the most important of which cover the manage-ment of hypertension associated with chronic kidney disease
(KDIGO Guideline for the Management of Blood Pressure in
CKD: https://kdigo.org/guidelines/blood-pressure-in-ckd/ ).
At the end of each chapter, a research agenda has also beenincluded and is intended to provide a roadmap for futureinvestigation based on our comprehensive review of thecurrent state of clinical evidence.
The majority of glomerular diseases are classi ﬁed as rare
diseases, and consequently, there is a paucity of randomized
controlled trials on which to base ﬁrm recommendations.
Given this situation, evidence-based recommendations have
been supplemented with practice points, based on retro-spective analyses, registry data, and consensus of expertopinion to ﬁll in management gaps when there was insuf ﬁ-
cient evidence to make a formal recommendation. The readerwill notice that most of this guideline is comprised of practicepoints. This should be taken as a challenge to the clinical
investigators of the nephrology community to develop novel
clinical trial designs, such as basket trials, umbrella trials,biomarker-driven trials, and n-of-1 trials, to implement theproposed research agenda in the absence of a suf ﬁcient
number of patients to carry out traditional prospective ran-domiz
ed controlled trials.
As Co-Chairs, we are more than grateful to the Work
Group, Evidence Review Team, and KDIGO staff for their
outstanding contributions to the creation of this extensiveintroduction www.kidney-international.org
S28 Kidney International (2021) 100 , S1–S276guideline. The Work Group was diverse, multinational,
multidisciplinary, experienced, thoughtful, and dedicated,and volunteered countless hours of their time to developingthis guideline. Finally, we owe a special debt of gratitude to
the KDIGO Executive Committee, in particular Marcello
Tonelli, who reviewed the guideline and made very helpfulsuggestions on methodological aspects of this project.We hope that the guidance provided here will lead to better
and more standardized care and improved outcomes for pa-tients with immune-mediated glomerular diseases.

nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines several practice points related to the assessment and management of glomerular disease. Key points include:

1. Routine quantification of sodium excretion during timed urinary collections is unnecessary unless there are concerns about adherence to dietary sodium restrictions.
2. Proteinuria should be quantified in glomerular disease due to its significance for prognosis and treatment decisions, with qualitative assessments being useful in specific cases.
3. In children, proteinuria should be quantified with a target of less than 200 mg/g or 8 mg/m²/hour, and higher baseline levels should only be accepted with evidence of kidney scarring from a biopsy.
4. The preferred equations for estimating glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) differ by age, with CKD-EPI for adults and the modified Schwartz equation for children, while the Full Age Spectrum equation can be used for both.
5. Routine evaluation of urine sediment for erythrocyte morphology and red cell casts is recommended in all forms of glomerular disease, and monitoring hematuria may provide prognostic value, particularly in conditions like immunoglobulin A nephropathy and vasculitis.
6. The document also includes management strategies for complications associated with glomerular disease, such as edema management in nephrotic syndrome.

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines key practice points regarding the management of patients with nephrotic syndrome (NS) and glomerular disease. It emphasizes anticoagulant dosing considerations specific to nephrotic syndrome, highlighting the need for careful management due to the associated risks. It recommends vaccinations for pneumococcus, influenza, and herpes zoster for patients with glomerular disease and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Additionally, it advises screening for various infections, including tuberculosis and hepatitis viruses, particularly in patients receiving immunosuppression. The document also discusses the importance of considering Strongyloides superinfection in certain patients and suggests prophylactic use of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for those on high-dose immunosuppressive therapy. Furthermore, it addresses outcome measures, indicating that goals for proteinuria reduction differ based on the specific causes of glomerular disease and suggests a decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) as a surrogate measure for kidney failure. Lastly, it includes considerations for pediatric patients with glomerulonephritis regarding venous thromboembolism and bleeding risk.

Immunoglobulin A nephropathy
2.1 Diagnosis
Practice Point 2.1.1: Considerations for the diagnosis of immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN):
/C15IgAN can only be diagnosed with a kidney biopsy.
/C15Determine the MEST-C score (mesangial [M] and endocapillary [E] hypercellularity, segmental sclerosis [S], inter-
stitial ﬁbrosis/tubular atrophy [T], and crescents [C]) according to the revised Oxford Classi ﬁcation.80
/C15There are no validated diagnostic serum or urine biomarkers for IgAN.
/C15Assess all patients with IgAN for secondary causes.
2.2 Prognosis
Practice Point 2.2.1: Considerations for the prognostication of primary IgAN:
/C15Clinical and histologic data at the time of biopsy can be used to risk stratify patients.
/C15The International IgAN Prediction Tool is a valuable resource to quantify risk of progression and inform shared
decision-making with patients.
BCalculate by QxMD
/C15The International IgAN Prediction Tool incorporates clinical information at the time of biopsy and cannot be used to
determine the likely impact of any particular treatment regimen.
/C15There are no validated prognostic serum or urine biomarkers for IgAN other than eGFR and proteinuria.
2.3 Treatment
Practice Point 2.3.1: Considerations for treatment of all patients with IgAN who do not have a variant form of primary
IgAN:
/C15The primary focus of management should be optimized supportive care.
/C15Assess cardiovascular risk and commence appropriate interventions as necessary.
/C15Give lifestyle advice, including information on dietary sodium restriction, smoking cessation, weight control, and
exercise, as appropriate.
/C15Other than dietary sodium restriction, no speci ﬁc dietary intervention has been shown to alter outcomes in IgAN.
/C15Variant forms of IgAN: IgA deposition with minimal change disease (MCD), IgAN with acute kidney injury (AKI),
and IgAN with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) may require speci ﬁc immediate treatment.www.kidney-international.org summary of recommendation sta tements and practice points

The partial document covers Chapter 2, focusing on Immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) and Immunoglobulin A vasculitis (IgAV). It outlines key points regarding the diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment of IgAN. 

1. **Diagnosis**: IgAN can only be confirmed through a kidney biopsy, and the MEST-C score is used for classification. There are no validated serum or urine biomarkers for diagnosis, and secondary causes must be assessed.

2. **Prognosis**: Clinical and histologic data at biopsy can help in risk stratification. The International IgAN Prediction Tool is highlighted as a resource for quantifying progression risk, although it does not predict treatment impact. Validated prognostic biomarkers are limited to eGFR and proteinuria.

3. **Treatment**: Management should focus on supportive care, cardiovascular risk assessment, and lifestyle modifications. Specific dietary interventions beyond sodium restriction are not proven to affect outcomes. For patients with proteinuria greater than 0.5 g/d, treatment with either an ACE inhibitor or ARB is recommended, regardless of hypertension status. The document also mentions variant forms of IgAN that may require immediate treatment. 

Overall, the chapter emphasizes the importance of a comprehensive approach to diagnosing, prognosticating, and treating IgAN.

S42 Kidney International (2021) 100 , S1–S2762.3.1 Patients with IgAN who are at high risk of progressive CKD despite maximal supportive care
Practice Point 2.3.1.1: Considerations for treatment of patients with IgAN who are at high risk of progressive CKD despite
maximal supportive care.
/C15High risk of progression in IgAN is currently de ﬁned as proteinuria >0.75 –1 g/d despite ‡90 days of optimized
supportive care.
/C15Immunosuppressive drugs should be considered only in patients with IgAN who remain at high risk of progressive
CKD despite maximal supportive care (The patients enrolled in the only large randomized controlled trial [RCT]
suggesting bene ﬁt of immunosuppression had an average of 2.4 g/d of proteinuria).
/C15In view of the current uncertainty over the safety and ef ﬁcacy of existing immunosuppressive treatment choices, all
patients who remain at high risk of progressive CKD despite maximal supportive care should be offered the op-
portunity to take part in a clinical trial.
/C15In all patients in whom immunosuppression is being considered, a detailed discussion of the risks and bene ﬁts of
each drug should be undertaken with the patient recognizing that adverse treatment effects are more likely in patientswith an eGFR <50 ml/min per 1.73 m
2.
/C15There is insuf ﬁcient evidence to support the use of the Oxford Classi ﬁcation MEST-C score in determining whether
immunosuppression should be commenced in IgAN.
/C15There is insuf ﬁcient evidence to base treatment decisions on the presence and number of crescents in the kidney
biopsy.
/C15The International IgAN Prediction Tool cannot be used to determine the likely impact of any particular treatmentregimen.
/C15Dynamic assessment of patient risk over time should be performed, as decisions regarding immunosuppression maychange.
Practice Point 2.3.1.2: Proteinuria reduction to under 1 g/d is a surrogate marker of improved kidney outcome in IgAN,
and reduction to under 1 g/d is a reasonable treatment target.
Recommendation 2.3.1.1: We suggest that patients who remain at high risk of progressive CKD despite
maximal supportive care be considered for a 6-month course of glucocorticoid
therapy. The important risk of treatment-emergent toxicity must be discussed with
patients, particularly those who have an eGFR <50 ml/min per 1.73 m
2(2B).www.kidney-international.org summary of recommendation sta tements and practice points

nodes.title: Practice Point 1.2.8: In children, quantify proteinuria, but goals of treatment should not be different between disease etiologies. A PCR of <200 mg/g (<20 mg/mmol) or <8 mg/m2/hour in a 24-hour urine should be the goal for any child with glomerular disease. Acceptance of a baseline higher than this should come only with kidney biopsy evidence of kidney scarring.
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the management of patients with IgA Nephropathy (IgAN) who are at high risk of progressive chronic kidney disease (CKD) despite receiving maximal supportive care. Key points include the definition of high risk based on proteinuria levels, the consideration of immunosuppressive drugs only for those who remain at high risk, and the importance of clinical trials due to uncertainties regarding the safety and efficacy of these treatments. It emphasizes the need for detailed discussions about the risks and benefits of immunosuppression, particularly in patients with reduced kidney function. The document also highlights that there is insufficient evidence to support certain classification systems and treatment decisions based on kidney biopsy findings. Additionally, it suggests that reducing proteinuria to under 1 g/d is a reasonable treatment target and recommends considering a 6-month course of glucocorticoid therapy for high-risk patients, while cautioning about potential toxicity. The clinical benefit of glucocorticoids is not well established, and their use should be approached with caution, particularly in specific situations outlined in the document.

The partial document discusses various treatment approaches and considerations for immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN). Key points include:

1. **Pharmacologic Therapies**: It mentions other pharmacologic therapies evaluated for IgAN, highlighting the role of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi), angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARB), and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF).

2. **Tonsillectomy**: The document states that tonsillectomy should not be performed as a treatment for IgAN in Caucasian patients, although some guidelines suggest it for recurrent tonsillitis in IgAN patients. Studies from Japan indicate potential benefits of tonsillectomy in improving kidney survival and reducing hematuria and proteinuria.

3. **IgAN with Nephrotic Syndrome**: It describes the rare occurrence of nephrotic syndrome in IgAN, the association with mesangial IgA deposition, and the need for treatment according to minimal change disease (MCD) guidelines if specific features are present.

4. **IgAN with Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)**: The document outlines the management of AKI in IgAN, particularly in cases of severe hematuria, and emphasizes the importance of kidney biopsy if kidney function does not improve.

5. **IgAN with Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN)**: It defines rapidly progressive IgAN and the necessity of kidney biopsy to confirm the diagnosis. Treatment recommendations include cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids, following guidelines for AAV.

Overall, the document provides clinical practice points for managing IgAN in various contexts, emphasizing the importance of tailored treatment based on specific patient presentations.

/C15IgAN is a disease predominantly of young adults, and all women of childbearing potential should be offered pre-
conception counseling when appropriate.
/C15Preconception counseling should include a discussion on cessation of renin –angiotensin system (RAS) blockade.
Blood pressure control should be optimized with alternative antihypertensive medications prior to conception.
/C15In those women at high risk of progressive CKD (Recommendation 2.3.1.1) despite maximal supportive care, a trial of
immunosuppression to optimize immunologic activity and reduce proteinuria prior to conception may be preferableto emergent initiation of immunosuppression during pregnancy.
Practice Point 2.4.5: IgAN in children:
General considerations
/C15For the purposes of this practice point, children are deﬁ ned as those aged <18 years. It is acknowledged that post-
pubertal children in some respects may have a similar course and response to treatment as adults with IgAN, butthere are insuf ﬁcient data currently to recommend that they be managed as adults with IgAN.
/C15Visible hematuria is more frequent in children than in adults, and this may account for earlier diagnosis inchildren.
126
/C15Children generally have higher eGFR, lower urine protein excretion, and more hematuria than adults at diagnosis.127
Kidney biopsy in children
/C15A kidney biopsy is usually performed at presentation of symptoms (hematuria, proteinuria, normal C3) in order toconﬁrm the diagnosis (and rule out other diagnoses) and assess the degree of in ﬂammation/presence of necrosis.
/C15Inﬂammation, mesangial, and endocapillary hypercellularity tend to be more prevalent in kidney biopsies of IgAN in

/C15There is strong evidence suggesting a bene ﬁt of RAS blockade in children.132All children with IgAN and proteinuria
>200 mg/d or PCR >200 mg/g ( >0.2 g/g [20 mg/mmol]) should receive ACEi or ARB blockade, advice on a low-
sodium diet, and optimal lifestyle and blood pressure control (systolic blood pressure [SBP] <90th percentile for
age, sex, and height).
/C15It is widely acknowledged that treatment of IgAN with immunosuppression differs between adults and children, andthat in children, the use of immunosuppressants is more widespread, particularly the use of glucocorticoids. How-ever, RCTs and speci ﬁc expert consensus-driven indications are lacking.
/C15Evidence derived mostly from retrospective studies suggests that treatment with glucocorticoids (plus second-lineimmunosuppression) leads to improved kidney survival.
126,133
/C15In children with proteinuria >1 g/d or PCR >1 g/g (100 mg/mmol) and/or mesangial hypercellularity, most pediatric
nephrologists will treat with glucocorticoids in addition to RAS blockade from time of diagnosis. Duration of treatmentis not established, but usually 4 weeks of 1 –2 mg/kg/d of oral prednisolone (or equivalent) followed by alternate-day
tapering over 4-6 months is employed. Regimens including intravenous methylprednisolone are also used.
127,128,130,134
/C15Evidence for the use of non-glucocorticoid immunosuppressants in addition to glucocorticoids is scarce, but thisapproach may be considered in more severe cases.
/C15As for adults, IgAN with MCD may be found, and it should be treated as steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome (SSNS;Chapter 4).
/C15As in adults, children with rapidly progressive IgAN have a poor outcome, and despite limited evidence, thissubgroup should be offered treatment with glucocorticoids (usually as methylprednisolone pulses) andcyclophosphamide.
128,130,135
Follow-up
/C15Aim for proteinuria £200 mg/d ( £400 mg/1.73 m2/d) or PCR £200 mg/g ( £0.2 g/g [ £20 mg/mmol]).
/C15Aim for blood pressure at SBP <90th percentile for age, sex, and height.
/C15Continue to follow patients even after complete remission, as they can relapse even after many years.136summary of recommendation sta tements and practice points www.kidney-international.org

6. **Follow-Up Care**: Stresses the importance of ongoing monitoring for proteinuria and blood pressure in patients, even after remission.

8. **IgAV Treatment**: Provides recommendations for managing IgAV-associated nephritis, including lifestyle interventions and blood pressure management, while cautioning against glucocorticoids for prevention in isolated cases.
9. **Special Situations**: Discusses the management of IgAV with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) and the potential role of plasma exchange in severe cases.

Overall, the document serves as a guideline for healthcare professionals in managing IgAN and IgAV, emphasizing tailored treatment approaches based on patient demographics and clinical presentations.

2.5 Diagnosis
Practice Point 2.5.1: Considerations for the diagnosis of immunoglobulin A vasculitis (IgAV):
/C15Unlike children, there are no internationally agreed upon criteria for the diagnosis of IgAV in adults, although a
clinical diagnosis of IgAV is often made based on the criteria described for children.140,141
/C15In adults with a vasculitic rash typical of IgAV, a kidney biopsy should be performed in the setting of featuresconsistent with a persistent and/or signi ﬁcant nephritis, RPGN, proteinuria >1g/d, and/or impaired kidney function.
/C15Assess all adult patients with IgAV for secondary causes.
/C15Assess all adult patients with IgAV for malignancy, with age- and sex-appropriate screening tests.

Practice Point 2.6.1: Considerations for the prognostication of IgAV:
/C15Retrospective data from a limited number of small registries have identi ﬁed uncontrolled hypertension and the
amount of proteinuria at presentation, and hypertension and mean proteinuria during follow-up, as predictors of a
poor kidney outcome in adults with IgAV.142–144
/C15The Oxford Classi ﬁcation has not been validated for IgAV.
/C15The International IgAN Prediction Tool88is not designed for prognostication in IgAV.
2.7 Treatment
2.7.1 Prevention of nephritis in IgAV
Recommendation 2.7.1.1: We recommend not using glucocorticoids to prevent nephritis in patients with iso-
lated extrarenal IgAV (1B).
Practice Point 2.7.1.1: Considerations for the treatment of all patients with IgAV-associated nephritis (IgAVN) who do not
have an RPGN:
/C15Assess cardiovascular risk and commence appropriate interventions as necessary.
/C15Give lifestyle advice, including information on smoking cessation, weight control, and exercise, as appropriate.
/C15No speci ﬁc dietary intervention has been shown to alter outcomes in IgAVN.
/C15Treat to nationally agreed-upon blood pressure targets. KDIGO suggests treating to an SBP target of <120 mm Hg
measured using standardized of ﬁce blood pressure measurement ( Figure 8).
/C15Treat with maximally tolerated dose of ACEi or ARB if proteinuria >0.5 g/d.
/C15Offer participation in a clinical trial if one is available.
2.7.2 Patients with IgAVN who are at high risk of progressive CKD despite maximal supportive care
Practice Point 2.7.2.1: Considerations for the treatment of patients with IgAVN who are at high risk of progressive CKD
despite maximal supportive care:
/C15There is insuf ﬁcient evidence to support the use of the Oxford Classi ﬁcation MEST-C score in determining whether
immunosuppression should be commenced in patients with IgAVN.
/C15The presence of crescents in the kidney biopsy is not in itself an automatic indication for commencement of
immunosuppression.
/C15In all patients in whom immunosuppression is being considered, a detailed discussion of the risks and bene ﬁts of
each drug should be undertaken with the patient with a recognition that adverse treatment effects are more likely in
patients with an eGFR <50 ml/min per 1.73 m2.

for IgAN.

/C15The potential risks and bene ﬁts of immunosuppression should be evaluated at the individual patient level and
discussed with the patient.

The partial document discusses the diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment of Immunoglobulin A vasculitis (IgAV), particularly in adults and children. Key points include:

1. **Diagnosis**: There are no internationally agreed criteria for diagnosing IgAV in adults, and diagnosis often relies on pediatric criteria. Kidney biopsies are recommended for adults with significant nephritis features. Secondary causes and malignancy should be assessed in all adult patients.

2. **Prognosis**: Factors such as uncontrolled hypertension and proteinuria levels at presentation are identified as predictors of poor kidney outcomes in adults. Existing classification tools like the Oxford Classification and the International IgAN Prediction Tool are not validated for IgAV.

3. **Treatment**: 
   - Glucocorticoids are not recommended for preventing nephritis in patients with isolated extrarenal IgAV.
   - For patients with IgAV-associated nephritis (IgAVN), cardiovascular risk should be assessed, and lifestyle modifications encouraged. Blood pressure should be managed according to national guidelines.
   - Immunosuppression considerations for high-risk patients are discussed, emphasizing the need for a detailed risk-benefit discussion before treatment.

4. **Special Situations**: The document addresses IgAV with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN), highlighting the need for individualized treatment plans and the potential role of plasma exchange in severe cases.

5. **IgAV in Children**: Management guidelines for children with IgAVN are outlined, noting that glucocorticoids are not supported for preventing nephritis in those with mild kidney involvement. Monitoring and treatment protocols for children are specified, including the use of ACE inhibitors for persistent proteinuria.

Overall, the document provides a comprehensive overview of IgAV, focusing on diagnostic criteria, prognostic factors, treatment recommendations, and special considerations for both adults and children.

nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses guidelines and practice points related to the management of IgA vasculitis (IgAV) and membranous nephropathy (MN). It emphasizes the following main points:

1. **IgAV in Children**: 
   - Defines children as individuals under 18 years and notes the lack of sufficient data to treat post-pubertal children as adults with IgA nephropathy (IgAN).
   - Highlights that glucocorticoids are not supported for preventing nephritis in children with mild or absent kidney involvement.
   - Notes that children over 10 years often present with non-nephrotic-range proteinuria and impaired kidney function, and that most will develop nephritis within three months of presentation.
   - Recommends urinary monitoring for at least six months and treatment with ACE inhibitors or ARBs for those with persistent proteinuria.
   - Advises kidney biopsy for children with significant proteinuria or impaired kidney function and suggests treatment options for those with moderate IgAV nephritis.

2. **Membranous Nephropathy**:
   - States that a kidney biopsy is not necessary to confirm MN diagnosis if anti-PLA2R antibodies are positive.
   - Recommends evaluating patients for associated conditions regardless of antibody presence.
   - Discusses the prognosis of MN, emphasizing the use of clinical and laboratory criteria to assess the risk of progressive kidney function loss, including the importance of eGFR and serum creatinine levels.
   - Suggests monitoring anti-PLA2R antibody levels and their changes as part of risk estimation and treatment decisions.

Overall, the document provides clinical recommendations for the diagnosis, management, and prognosis of IgAV in children and MN in patients.

2.8.1 IgAV-associated nephritis in children
Practice Point 2.8.1.1: For the purposes of this practice point, children are de ﬁned as those aged <18 years. It is
acknowledged that post-pubertal children in some respects may have a similar course and
response to treatment as adults with IgAN, but there are insuf ﬁcient data currently to recommend
that they be managed as adults with IgAN. Indications for management of IgAVN in children haverecently been published as the result of a European consortium initiative.
140Brieﬂy:
/C15There are no data supporting the use of glucocorticoids to prevent nephritis in children with IgAV but mild orabsent evidence of kidney involvement.
153,154
/C15Children >10 years of age more often present with non-nephrotic-range proteinuria and impaired kidney function,
and they may suffer more chronic histologic lesions with delay in biopsy and delay in treatment longer than 30 days.155
/C15The majority of children who will develop nephritis will do so within 3 months of presentation. Urinary monitoringis necessary for ‡6 months and optimally 12 months from initial presentation of systemic disease.
/C15Children with IgAVN and persistent proteinuria for >3 months should be treated with an ACEi or ARB. A pediatric
nephrologist should be consulted.
/C15A kidney biopsy should be performed in children with nephrotic-range proteinuria, impaired GFR, or persistentmoderate ( >1 g/d) proteinuria.
/C15Oral prednisone/prednisolone or pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone should be used in children with mild ormoderate IgAVN.
/C15Children with IgAVN with nephrotic syndrome and/or rapidly deteriorating kidney function are treated in the sameway as those with rapidly progressive IgAN.

The partial document discusses the prognosis and treatment considerations for patients with Membranous Nephropathy (MN). It emphasizes the importance of using clinical and laboratory criteria, such as estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and serum creatinine (SCr) levels, to assess the risk of progressive kidney function loss. The document outlines specific thresholds for SCr and eGFR, highlighting the need to consider age when interpreting these values. It also mentions the monitoring of anti-PLA2R antibodies as a key factor in risk estimation and treatment response.

In terms of treatment, the document recommends that all patients with primary MN and proteinuria receive optimal supportive care, while immunosuppressive therapy should be reserved for those at risk of progressive kidney injury. It specifies that immunosuppressive therapy is not necessary for patients with lower levels of proteinuria and normal kidney function unless risk factors or serious complications are present. For patients at risk, it suggests treatment options such as rituximab or cyclophosphamide, with a focus on monitoring anti-PLA2R antibody levels to guide therapy adjustments. The document also notes the potential for spontaneous remission in patients with moderate risk and normal eGFR.

Practice Point 3.3.1: Considerations for treatment of patients with primary MN:
/C15All patients with primary MN and proteinuria should receive optimal supportive care.
/C15Immunosuppressive therapy should be restricted to patie nts considered at risk for progressive kidney injury (Figure 31 ).
Practice Point 3.3.2: Immunosuppressive therapy is not required in patients with MN, proteinuria <3.5 g/d, serum al-
bumin >30 g/l by bromocresol purple (BCP) or immunometric assay, and eGFR >60 ml/min per
1.73 m2.
Practice Point 3.3.3: Immunosuppressive therapy is not required in patients with MN, nephrotic syndrome, and normal
eGFR, unless at least one risk factor for disease progression is present or serious complications of
nephrotic syndrome (e.g., AKI, infections, thromboembolic events) have occurred.
Recommendation 3.3.1: For patients with MN and at least one risk factor for disease progression, we recom-
mend using rituximab or cyclophosphamide and alternate month glucocorticoids for 6
months, or CNI-based therapy for ‡6 months, with the choice of treatment depending
on the risk estimate ( Figure 30 and Figure 31) (1B).
Practice Point 3.3.4: Longitudinal monitoring of anti-PLA2R antibody levels at 6 months after start of therapy may be
useful for evaluating treatment response in patients with MN, and can be used to guide adjustments
to therapy ( Figure 33193).
Figure 31 | Risk-based treatment of MN.*See Practice Point 3.2.1 and Figure 30 for a detailed description of risk evaluation.†Calcineurin
inhibitor (CNI) monotherapy is considered less efﬁ cient. Treatment with CNI for 6 –12 months with rapid withdrawal is associated with a high
relapse rate. Still, its use may be considered in patients with normal eGFR and moderate risk of progression, since many of these patients will
develop a spontaneous remission. The use of CNI will shorten the period of proteinuria. In patients with high risk of progression, additionof rituximab after 6 months of treatment with CNI is advised, with the possible exception of patients with documented disappearance ofanti-PLA2R antibodies after CNI treatment.
‡There is insuf ﬁcient evidence that rituximab used in standard doses prevents development of
kidney failure. If eGFR falls below 50 ml/min per 1.73 m2, the doses of cyclophosphamide should be halved. In patients who do not tolerate or
can no longer use cyclophosphamide, rituximab could be offered. nodes.title: Practice Point 1.7.1: Full anticoagulation is indicated for patients with thromboembolic events occurring in the context of nephrotic syndrome. Prophylactic anticoagulation should be employed in patients with nephrotic syndrome when the risk of thromboembolism exceeds the estimated patient-specific risks of an anticoagulation-induced serious bleeding event.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines treatment considerations for patients with primary membranous nephropathy (MN). Key points include:

1. **Supportive Care**: All patients with primary MN and proteinuria should receive optimal supportive care, while immunosuppressive therapy is reserved for those at risk of progressive kidney injury.

2. **Immunosuppressive Therapy Criteria**: Immunosuppressive therapy is not necessary for patients with proteinuria less than 3.5 g/d, normal serum albumin, and adequate kidney function (eGFR >60 ml/min). It is also not required in cases of nephrotic syndrome with normal eGFR unless risk factors for progression or serious complications arise.

3. **Recommended Treatments**: For patients with MN and at least one risk factor for progression, treatment options include rituximab or cyclophosphamide combined with glucocorticoids, or calcineurin inhibitor (CNI)-based therapy for at least six months, depending on risk assessment.

4. **Monitoring Treatment Response**: Longitudinal monitoring of anti-PLA2R antibody levels is suggested to evaluate treatment response and guide therapy adjustments.

5. **Management of Relapse**: An algorithm for managing initial relapse after therapy is provided, emphasizing the importance of immunologic monitoring and the evaluation of anti-PLA2R antibodies during remission and relapse.

6. **Cumulative Dose Considerations**: The document highlights the importance of not exceeding cumulative doses of cyclophosphamide to mitigate risks of malignancy and fertility concerns.

Overall, the document emphasizes a risk-based approach to treatment and monitoring in patients with MN, focusing on individualized care based on disease progression and response to therapy.

Practice Point 3.4.1: Algorithm for the treatment of patients with MN and initial relapse after therapy ( Figure 34 )
Figure 33 | Immunologic monitoring in MN after start of therapy. See text for current treatment schedu les. Note: The cumulative dose of
cyclophosphamide should not exceed 36 g in view of the risk of malignancy (Ch apter 1). To stay on the safe side, we usually limit the cumulative dose to 25
g (in an 80 kg male: 6 months cyclical cyclophosphamide at a dose of 2.5 mg/kg/d equals 18 g and 6 months daily cyclophosphamide at a dose of 1.5 mg/
kg/d equals 22 g). Lower doses (maximum 10 g) must be used in patients who wish to conceive. CNI are unlikely to induce late immunologic remission; in

of rituximab therapy; extra doses may be considered even if B cells in the peripheral blood are absent o r very low. However, in these patients, consulta tion
with an expert center is advised. eGFR should be stable; if not, then it is always necessary to evaluate for other ca uses, and if eGFR decrease is attribu ted to
MN activity, always provide additional therapy.*Some centers will measure anti-PLA2R antibodies a t month 3, and adapt treatment at that time. In most
patients, response occurs within 3 months after start of therapy.†A negative immuno ﬂuorescence test indicates immunologic remission. If measured by

Figure 34 | Management of initial relapse after therapy in MN. Details of commonly used treat ment regimens are shown in Figure 32.*The
deﬁnition of relapse is variable. Some authors de ﬁne relapse after remission as an increase in proteinuria >3.5 g/d in patients who developed a partial or
complete remission. We suggest that the course o f serum albumin and PCR should be used in the evaluation. If PCR decreased to values between 2 –3.5 g/
d without an increase of serum albumin to normal, the subsequent rise in PCR s hould be considered resistant diseas e rather than relapse after remissio n.

by a decrease in serum albumin levels.†Immunologic monitoring is of particularly great value in these situations. If, in the period of “clinical remission, ”
anti-PLA2R antibodies were still positive, this w ould be evidence for resistant disease. Therefore , in patients with positive anti-PLA2R antibodi es, it is
advised that anti-PLA2R antibodies b e evaluated at the time of remission and relapse. The cour se of anti-PLA2R antibodies should precede the clinica l

Patients and household contacts should receive the influenza vaccine. Patients should receive herpes zoster vaccination (Shingrix).
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the evaluation and management of patients with membranous nephropathy (MN), particularly in the context of kidney transplant recipients and children. It highlights the importance of assessing the risk of clinical recurrence of MN, especially in relation to the THSD7A antigen/antibodies. The document outlines an algorithm for managing children with MN and emphasizes the need for careful consideration of prophylactic anticoagulant therapy in patients with MN and nephrotic syndrome. Key points include the relationship between serum albumin levels and thrombotic risk, the assessment of venous and arterial thrombotic events, and the use of anticoagulants like warfarin and low-molecular-weight heparin. It also notes the increased risk of thrombosis associated with glucocorticoid therapy and provides guidance on using the Framingham risk score for estimating arterial thromboembolism risk.

Should aspirin be used for primary prevention of thrombotic events in patients with membranous nephropathy? Pages 981 –983, Copyright
Copyright 2016, with permission from the International Society of Nephrology.44Proposed algorithm for anticoagulant therapy in patients with
membranous nephropathy (MN). This algorithm provides guidance for the clinicians. The proposed cutoff values are based on expert opinion.
When considering anticoagulant therapy, it is important to balance bene ﬁts and risks. The following are important considerations:
1. The risk of thrombotic events is related to the level of serum albumin. It is important to note that there is a large difference among the
serum albumin assays.204A serum albumin concentration of 25 g/l (2.5 g/dl) with bromocresol green (BCG) equals a concentration of
w20 g/l (2.0 g/dl) with bromocresol purple (BCP), or immunonephelometry. It is likely that most studies have used the BCG assay. Consider
using 25 g/l (2.5 g/dl) as a threshold when using BCG, and 20 g/l (2.0 g/dl) when using BCP or immunonephelometry.
2. Assess risk of venous thrombosis and risk of bleeding ( https://www.med.unc.edu/gntools/bleedrisk.html ).
3. Patients with MN and nephrotic syndrome are also at risk of developing arterial thrombotic events. The risk of arterial thromboembolism
(ATE) is dependent on age, history of previous events, diabetes, estimated glomerular ﬁltration rate (eGFR), smoking, and severity of
nephrotic syndrome (NS). Risk assessment can be done using the Framingham risk score, and including previous events and proteinuria.44
4. Use of aspirin is insuf ﬁcient to prevent venous thromboembolism (VTE); use of warfarin is suf ﬁcient to prevent ATE.
5. Treatment with warfarin: There is more international normalized ratio (INR) variability in nephrotic syndrome and low eGFR; there is increased
risk of thrombosis immediately after starting high-dose warfarin. Consider starting anticoagulation therapy with low-dose low-molecular-
weight heparin and then folding-in warfarin and, when therapeutic, stopping the heparin. A good alternative is to use low-dose low-mo-
lecular-weight heparin þaspirin for a period of 3 months before switching to warfarin, allowing for judgment on the course of proteinuria.205
6. Glucocorticoids increase the risk of thrombosis; thus, anticoagulant therapy should not be omitted in patients who start prednisone therapy.7. ATE risk is estimated using the Framingham risk score, with added risk in case of low eGFR or higher proteinuria. The Framingham risk
score takes into account age, smoking, serum cholesterol, and blood pressure.

nodes.summary:
The partial document covers Chapter 4 on nephrotic syndrome in children, focusing on three main areas: diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment. 

1. **Diagnosis**: It emphasizes the clinical characteristics used to define nephrotic syndrome in children aged 1-18 years, including the importance of collecting first morning urine to rule out orthostatic proteinuria.

2. **Prognosis**: The prognosis is primarily determined by the child's response to initial treatment and the frequency of relapses within the first year. A kidney biopsy is generally not required at the initial presentation unless there is resistance to therapy or an atypical clinical course.

3. **Treatment**: 
   - **Initial Treatment**: The document recommends a regimen of oral glucocorticoids for 8 to 12 weeks, detailing specific dosing guidelines.
   - **Prevention and Treatment of Relapses**: It outlines strategies for managing relapses, including the use of glucocorticoids during infections and the introduction of glucocorticoid-sparing agents for children with frequent relapses or steroid dependency. The choice of glucocorticoid-sparing agents is advised to be tailored to individual patient needs, considering factors like adherence and potential side effects. 

Overall, the document provides a comprehensive overview of the management of nephrotic syndrome in children, emphasizing evidence-based recommendations and practice points.

Chapter 4: Nephrotic syndrome in children
4.1 Diagnosis
Practice Point 4.1.1: The de ﬁnitions relating to nephrotic syndrome in children are based on the clinical characteristics
outlined in Figure 39206.
Figure 39 | De ﬁnitions relating to NS in children aged 1 –18 years.*To rule out orthostatic proteinuria, the ﬁrst morning urine should be
collected separately for assessment.†van der Watt et al.206NS, nephrotic syndrome; PCR, protein-creatinine ratio; SRNS, steroid-resistant
nephrotic syndrome; SSNS, steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome.www.kidney-international.org summary of recommendation sta tements and practice points
Kidney International (2021) 100 , S1–S276 S574.2 Prognosis
Practice Point 4.2.1: The prognosis for childhood nephrotic syndrome is best predicted by the patient ’s response to initial
treatment and frequency of relapse during the ﬁrst year after treatment. Therefore, a kidney biopsy is
not usually needed at initial presentation, and instead is reserved for children with resistance to
therapy or an atypical clinical course.
4.3 Treatment
4.3.1 Initial treatment of NS in children
Recommendation 4.3.1.1: We recommend that oral glucocorticoids be given for 8 weeks (4 weeks of daily
glucocorticoids followed by 4 weeks of alternate-day glucocorticoids) or 12 weeks (6
weeks of daily glucocorticoids followed by 6 weeks of alternate-day glucocorticoids)(1B).
Practice Point 4.3.1.1: The standard dosing regimen for the initial treatment of nephrotic syndrome is daily oral prednisone/
prednisolone 60 mg/m2/d or 2 mg/kg/d (maximum 60 mg/d) for 4 weeks followed by alternate day
prednisone/prednisolone, 40 mg/m2, or 1.5 mg/kg (maximum of 50 mg) for other 4 weeks, or
prednisone/prednisolone 60 mg/m2/d (maximum 60 mg/d) for 6 weeks followed by alternate day
prednisone/prednisolone, 40 mg/m2, or 1.5 mg/kg (maximum of 50 mg), for other 6 weeks.
4.3.2 Prevention and treatment of relapses of NS in children
Recommendation 4.3.2.1: For children with frequently relapsing and steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome
who are currently taking alternate-day glucocorticoids or are off glucocorticoids, werecommend that daily glucocorticoids 0.5 mg/kg/d be given during episodes of upper
respiratory tract and other infections for 5– 7 days to reduce the risk of relapse (1C).
Practice Point 4.3.2.1: The initial approach to relapse should include oral prednisone/prednisolone as a single daily dose of
60 mg/m2/d or 2 mg/kg/d (maximum 60 mg/d) until the child remits completely for ‡3 days.
Practice Point 4.3.2.2: After achieving complete remission, reduce oral prednisone/prednisolone to 40 mg/m2or 1.5 mg/kg
(maximum 50 mg) on alternate days for ‡4 weeks.
Practice Point 4.3.2.3: For children with frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome or steroid-dependent nephrotic syn-
drome without glucocorticoid toxicity, the same glucocorticoid regimen may be employed in
subsequent relapses.
Practice Point 4.3.2.4: For children with frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome without serious glucocorticoid-related
adverse effects, low-dose alternate-day oral prednisone/prednisolone (optimally £0.5 mg/kg/d) can
be prescribed to prevent relapse.
Recommendation 4.3.2.2: For children with frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome who develop serious
glucocorticoid-related adverse effects and for all children with steroid-dependent
nephrotic syndrome, we recommend that glucocorticoid-sparing agents be pre-
scribed, rather than no treatment or continuation with glucocorticoid treatmentalone (1B).
Practice Point 4.3.2.5: Patients should ideally be in remission with glucocorticoids prior to the initiation of glucocorticoid-
sparing agents such as oral cyclophosphamide, levamisole, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), rituximab,
or calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs). Coadministration of glucocorticoids is recommended for ‡2w e e k s
following initiation of glucocorticoid-sparing treatment.
Practice Point 4.3.2.6: Choosing the most appropriate glucocorticoid-sparing agent from among oral cyclophosphamide, le-
vamisole, MMF, rituximab, and CNI is a decision that requires careful consideration of speci ﬁcp a t i e n t -
related issues such as resources, adhe rence, adverse effects, and patient preferences. Oral cyclophospha-
mide and levamisole may be preferable glucocorticoid-sparing therapies in frequently relapsing nephroticsyndrome. MMF, rituximab, CNIs, and to a lesser ext ent, oral cyclophosphamide may be preferable to
glucocorticoid-sparing therapies in childre n with steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome ( Figure 41
178).summary of recommendation sta tements and practice points www.kidney-international.org
S58 Kidney International (2021) 100 , S1–S276

It emphasizes that the prognosis is primarily determined by the patient's response to initial treatment and the frequency of relapses within the first year, suggesting that kidney biopsies are typically unnecessary at initial presentation unless there is resistance to therapy or an atypical clinical course. 

For initial treatment, the document recommends administering oral glucocorticoids for either 8 or 12 weeks, detailing specific dosing regimens. It also outlines strategies for preventing and treating relapses in children with frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent NS, including the use of daily glucocorticoids during infections and specific dosing adjustments after achieving remission. 

Furthermore, it advocates for glucocorticoid-sparing agents for children experiencing serious glucocorticoid-related adverse effects, emphasizing the importance of patient-specific considerations when selecting these agents. The document provides guidance on the coadministration of glucocorticoids with glucocorticoid-sparing treatments and discusses the careful selection of therapies based on individual patient needs and preferences.

nodes.summary: The partial document discusses treatment recommendations for children with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome (SSNS) and minimal change disease (MCD) in adults. It highlights the use of calcineurin inhibitors (CNI) such as cyclosporine and tacrolimus as second-line therapies for children with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome. The document emphasizes the importance of individualized dosing of CNIs, monitoring serum creatinine levels to avoid toxicity, and adjusting doses based on patient response. Additionally, it notes that MCD in adults requires a kidney biopsy for diagnosis, and long-term kidney survival is favorable for those responding to glucocorticoids, with high-dose oral glucocorticoids recommended for initial treatment. The document also mentions that a kidney biopsy may not be necessary if there is a clear extrarenal cause for proteinuria.

nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines treatment guidelines for Minimal Change Disease (MCD) and Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) in adults. Key points include:

1. **Initial Treatment of MCD**: An algorithm is provided for the initial treatment of MCD, emphasizing high-dose glucocorticoid therapy for a maximum of 16 weeks, with tapering starting two weeks after achieving complete remission. The administration route and frequency of glucocorticoids can be tailored to individual patient needs.

2. **Alternative Therapies**: For patients where glucocorticoids are contraindicated, alternative treatments such as cyclophosphamide, calcineurin inhibitors (CNI), or mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) should be considered.

3. **Management of Relapses**: Guidelines for treating relapses are discussed, including the use of glucocorticoids for infrequent relapses and recommending cyclophosphamide, rituximab, CNIs, or mycophenolic acid analogs for frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent MCD.

4. **Diagnosis of FSGS**: The document also addresses the diagnosis of FSGS, highlighting the importance of differentiating between primary and secondary causes, particularly in adults without nephrotic syndrome.

Overall, the document provides a structured approach to the management of MCD and FSGS, emphasizing individualized treatment plans and the importance of evaluating underlying causes in FSGS cases.

The partial document covers recommendations and practice points related to the management of steroid-resistant primary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and infection-related glomerulonephritis (GN). Key points include:

1. **Steroid-Resistant Primary FSGS**: It is recommended that adults with this condition be treated with cyclosporine or tacrolimus for at least six months instead of glucocorticoid monotherapy. A suggested dosing schedule for these medications is provided.

2. **Duration of Treatment**: For those who respond to calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs), a minimum treatment duration of 12 months is advised to reduce relapse risk.

3. **Management of Resistance or Intolerance**: Patients who are resistant to or intolerant of CNIs should be referred to specialized centers for further evaluation, including potential rebiopsy or alternative treatments.

4. **Management of Relapse**: Adults with previous steroid-sensitive FSGS who experience a relapse can be treated similarly to those with relapsing minimal change disease (MCD).

5. **Infection-Related Glomerulonephritis**: The document emphasizes the utility of kidney biopsy in diagnosing bacterial infection-related GN, especially when culture results are inconclusive, to aid in prognosis and treatment decisions. 

Figures referenced in the document provide visual aids for treatment protocols and diagnostic evaluations.

It outlines practice points and recommendations for diagnosing and managing these conditions. Key points include:

2. **HCV-related GN**: The document aligns with KDIGO guidelines for the management of HCV in chronic kidney disease, emphasizing specific therapeutic recommendations.
3. **HBV-related GN**: It highlights the need for testing in patients with proteinuric glomerular disease, the risk of kidney failure in chronic HBV infection, and treatment recommendations involving nucleos(t)ide analogues. It advises against using pegylated interferon and cautions against immunosuppressive agents in untreated HBV cases.
4. **HIV-related GN**: The document recommends kidney biopsy for diagnosis, discusses factors affecting prognosis, and advocates for initiating antiretroviral therapy in all HIV patients with chronic kidney disease, particularly those with biopsy-proven HIV-associated nephropathy.

7.2.1 Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection –related GN
The Work Group concurs fully with Recommendations 5.1 –5.2.3 of the KDIGO 2018 Clinical Practice Guideline for the
Prevention, Diagnosis, Evaluation, and Treatment of Hepatitis C in Chronic Kidney Disease .405Please refer to this pub-
lication for speci ﬁc recommendations, selection, and dosing of speci ﬁc therapeutic agents, and research recommendations.
7.2.2 Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection –related GN
7.2.2.1 DiagnosisPractice Point 7.2.2.1.1: Patients with proteinuric glomerular disease should undergo testing for HBV infection.7.2.2.2 PrognosisPractice Point 7.2.2.2.1: Adult patients with chronic HBV infection should be considered at risk for the development of
kidney failure.
7.2.2.3 Treatment
Recommendation 7.2.2.3.1: We recommend that patients with replicative HBV infection (as denoted by HBV
DNA levels >2000 IU/ml) and GN receive treatment with nucleos(t)ide analogues as
recommended for the general population by standard clinical practice guidelines
for HBV infection (1C).
Practice Point 7.2.2.3.1: Pegylated interferon regimens should not be used to treat patients with replicative HBV infection
and GN.
Practice Point 7.2.2.3.2: Immunosuppressive agents, such as cyclophosphamide or rituximab, may accelerate HBV repli-
cation and should be avoided in patients with untreated replicative HBV infection and GN.
7.2.2.4 Special situations
Practice Point 7.2.2.4.1: Rituximab and cyclophosphamide should be avoided in patients with simultaneous HBV infection
and anti-PLA2R antibody –mediated MN until a sustained virologic remission has been obtained
by nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy.
Practice Point 7.2.2.4.2: Plasma exchange may be tried in patients with accompanying cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.
Practice Point 7.2.2.4.3: Children with HBV infection and MN should be managed conservatively without immuno-
suppression due to a high likelihood of spon taneous remission of the kidney disease.
7.2.3 Human immunode ﬁciency virus (HIV) –related GN
7.2.3.1 Diagnosis
Practice Point 7.2.3.1.1: A kidney biopsy should be performed, when feasible, to evaluate the morphology of HIV-related
kidney disease. A pathology-based description of HIV-related kidney disease should be used to
help de ﬁne and guide therapy.
7.2.3.2 Prognosis
Practice Point 7.2.3.2.1: The factors contributing to the long-term outcome of HIV infection associated with GN are
numerous and include persistence of viral replic ation, response to antiviral treatment, genetic
predisposition to glomerular injury (e.g., APOL1 risk alleles), coinfection with other viruses,
and development of immune complex disease or thrombotic microangiopathy. Thus, the esti-
mation of prognosis in individual patients can be very dif ﬁcult.
7.2.3.3 Treatment
Recommendation 7.2.3.3.1: We recommend that antiretroviral therapy be initiated in all patients with HIV and
CKD, especially biopsy-proven HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN), regardless of
CD4 count, adjusted to the degree of kidney function (1C).summary of recommendation sta tements and practice points www.kidney-international.org
S68 Kidney International (2021) 100 , S1–S276
